rounds.text: Revathi Equipment India Ltd is currently trading at a significant discount to its intrinsic value, with a margin of safety calculated at 60.6% [E38]. The market is currently pricing the stock for a modest 4.2% earnings growth, which stands in stark contrast to the company's historical 17% compounded profit growth and recent 21% growth in the trailing twelve months [E16, E17, E39]. This valuation gap is further highlighted by a P/E ratio of 14.5x and an EV/EBITDA of 8.83x, both of which are substantially lower than their respective sector benchmarks [E1, E6, E11]. Recent operational performance shows a sharp turnaround, with quarterly operating margins expanding by 12 percentage points year-over-year [E22]. Furthermore, the stock has regained technical momentum, currently trading above both its 50-day and 200-day moving averages [E42]. Conceded: the company faces challenges with negative operating cash flow, high debtor days, and inconsistent margin trends [E25, E26, E53, E54]. Despite these headwinds, the company operates within a sector currently experiencing a positive macro tailwind, supporting the potential for continued operational improvement [E60, E62].

Revathi Equipment India Ltd presents a concerning financial profile characterized by severe cash flow instability and deteriorating operational efficiency. The company reported negative operating cash flow of Rs -29 Cr and negative free cash flow of Rs -43 Cr in March 2026, resulting in a cash conversion ratio of -2.07x [E25, E26, E27]. This liquidity strain is compounded by a significant increase in borrowings, which rose from Rs 37 Cr to Rs 68 Cr over the same period [E31]. Furthermore, the company’s working capital management is weakening, with working capital days nearly doubling from 43.7 to 80.1 days and debtor days reaching an elevated 156 days [E53, E54]. While the company reports profits, these figures are bolstered by Rs 11.0 Cr in other income, and the firm fails to provide any dividend yield to shareholders [E51, E52]. Conceded: the company maintains a P/E ratio below the sector benchmark and shows positive institutional money flow [E6, E36]. Despite these metrics, the historical volatility remains extreme, evidenced by a record peak-to-trough drawdown of -85.5% and a negative Sharpe ratio of -0.99 [E45, E47].

The bear’s focus on cash flow [E25, E26, E27] ignores the company’s recent, dramatic operational turnaround, as evidenced by the 12 percentage point expansion in quarterly operating margins in June 2026 compared to the year-ago quarter [E22]. While the bear highlights rising borrowings [E31], it overlooks that the company is currently operating within a sector-wide capital goods tailwind [E60, E62] and is actively outperforming expectations, with profit growth now exceeding one-year price growth by 53% [E49]. Conceded: the company has high debtor days [E53] and negative cash conversion [E25]. However, the bear’s reliance on historical volatility [E45, E47] fails to account for the current technical strength, as the stock is now trading above both its 50-day and 200-day moving averages [E42]. Furthermore, the market is significantly under-pricing the company’s growth potential, as the current price implies only 4.2% earnings growth against a base case of 17% [E39]. Finally, the bear’s critique of dividend policy [E51] ignores that the company is reinvesting for growth, evidenced by a 21% compounded profit growth over the trailing twelve months [E17].

The bull’s reliance on a single quarter of margin expansion [E22] ignores the broader reality that the company’s yearly and quarterly operating-margin trends remain inconsistent [E23, E24]. While the bull points to technical strength [E42], it fails to reconcile this with the fact that the stock has suffered a 32.3% decline from its 52-week high [E41] and carries a negative Sharpe ratio of -0.99 [E47], indicating that recent price action has not compensated investors for the extreme 55.4% annualised volatility [E46]. Conceded: the company is trading above its moving averages [E42] and has seen profit growth [E17]. However, this profit growth is heavily reliant on "other income" of Rs 11.0 Cr [E52], which masks the underlying operational weakness evidenced by a massive negative operating cash flow of Rs -29 Cr [E26] and a cash conversion ratio of -2.07x [E25]. Furthermore, the bull’s claim that the company is reinvesting for growth is contradicted by the fact that working capital days have ballooned from 43.7 to 80.1 days [E54] and debtor days remain high at 156 [E53], suggesting that the company is struggling to collect on its sales rather than efficiently deploying capital. Finally, the bull ignores that the company’s long-term sales growth is a stagnant 2% [E14], which fundamentally undermines the sustainability of the 17% profit growth target [E39].
